samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Paul L. Carll was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Paul L. Carll. Mr. Carll served in the U.S. Army Air Corp with the 57th Fighter Group, 64th Squadron. Overseas, he served in the North African and the Mediterranean theaters and his highest rank was Captain. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Carll's home in Pepper Pike, Ohio, on February 11, 2003. Paul was 82 at the time of this recording. Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: I absolutely do. It's a fascinating story. The war was coming on. We knew that. Even our company was selling Bright Stock, Pennsylvania Bright Stock, to the Japanese in those times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's Bright Stock?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Bright Stock is the base for all motor oils and -- all lubricating oils. And some people were using it for gear lubricants. But in any case, we who worked at the company had discussions about how we were going to be sorry we were selling this stuff to them.

But, anyhow, the war rumors were flying, and since I was in the 19, 20, 21 age bracket, I knew that I was going to be eligible and probably drafted. Well, in 1939, the government started the CPT, which was Civilian Pilot Training program. And a good friend of mine in Franklin, he and I decided -- his name was Clare Ballard, and he and I decided that we didn't want to join a walking army, that we should try to get into the Air Corp in those days. And we talked about it.

So we took the CPT, the training program, and both of us graduated from that. We got our -- we got our pilot's license, private pilot's license, in the latter part of '39. And after we had learned to fly and in 1941, in March of '41, Ballard and I decided that we would try to go into the RCAF.

So we drove from Franklin, up to Hamilton, Ontario. And Hamilton, Ontario was the recruiting place for anybody who wanted to join up with the RCAF. Britain was already in the war, everything was going on over there. So anyhow, he and I drove up there. And went in, talked to them. And the deal was they didn't have anyplace to put new recruits. Everything was filled up.

So we would have to go to International Falls, Minnesota, the guard duty then between United States and Canada. And the pay was going to be 30 dollars, Canadian, a month. So we thanked them for all the information and went out. And Ballard said, "This isn't for us." And I agreed with him.

So it was about a four-hour drive or five-hour drive back down to Franklin from there. And on the way down we discussed what we -- what our next step would be. Neither one of us had a college education, but in those days, in Popular Science Magazine, the Air Corp was advertising for flying cadets. And the requirement was two years of college or passing an equivalency test. And you had to be minimum five-feet-four and weigh 115 pounds. Ballard had no trouble with that because he was a six-foot-two guy and weighing 185 pounds. But I was under 115. I only weighed about 110 pounds in those days.

So, anyhow, on the way back, we decided what we would do. We would try to take the test for two years of college and try to pass it. Now, what do we need for this? Well, I can remember the conversation as though it were yesterday. We decided that we could bluff our way through history. We could bluff our way through English. Our trouble was going to be mathematics, and we needed it for celestial navigation and that sort of thing. And so we said, "Well, why don't we get a tutor." I had only gone through plain geometry in high school and so had Clare. I said, "You know, if we could get a math teacher to tutor us for a while, maybe we could learn enough math to pass this sucker."

So I was delegated to find a math teacher. So I went into Oil City High School. There was a high school teacher there, his name was Coleman, and I explained what we needed and so on. Well, he -- that guy said, "Sure, I'll be happy to tutor you guys." And he said, "It will cost you 15 dollars a piece for the whole thing." And so we went to school with him. And he taught us all the way up through trigonometry and so on, and taught us how to handle the celestial navigation part. We did that for a couple of months. We worked -- we were really pretty diligent about studying. So then we went to the recruiter and got the papers and that sort of thing and told him that we wanted to take the test. We got word to take the test in August. I'm trying to answer your question about where --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, this is fine. Keep going.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: -- where I was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. This is August of '41.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Uh-huh. We went to the old post office building in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and we took the test. About a week or so later, we were notified we passed the test, both of us had passed it, and they sent us up to come in for the six-four physical exam.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Six-four physical?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: They called it six-four physical.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: It was just a name they called it, six-four. But it was really rigorous. I had had a paper route since I was 11 years old. It was five miles, and I walked around that thing every morning before school and I was in pretty good shape. We went down there, but my problem was with my weight. And so we went down to the -- this had to be in September of '41. We went there. The guy at the desk, his name was Larry Semans, Captain Larry Semans. I'll never forget the guy. We went in there and here's Ballard, he's six-two, and he says, "Okay, we'll arrange that." He looked at me and said, "You're too little. We're not going to test you." Well, I was devastated. So I argued. I told him I met the minimum requirements; five-four, I was five-four and I weighed 118 pounds. I said that, anyway.

So, no so, he wouldn't do it. So I waited on Ballard. He passed the test. So then I went back and I went back to work and I was devastated. And my boss told me, Tom Murphy, great guy, he said, "You can't put up with that kind of stuff," he said. "You meet the minimum requirement. You go back down there and point this out to him."

So a week later, I go back unannounced. I walk in. This Semans took one look at me, and he said, "I think I told you we weren't going to give you an examination, and we're not." So he says, "Don't waste your time coming down here and don't waste our time." Well, I said, "Okay." So I turn around and went back, and I told Tom this. He said, "You've got to go back down, Paul," he said. So I did. And I cut the article out of the Popular Science Magazine that gave all of the specifications and everything. And I went down there the third time. And I walked in and this guy said, told me -- by this time he knew me by name. And he said, "I thought I told you" -- we had a big argument. I pulled out this piece of paper there and I mean it was getting kind of loud in there, you know, and I pulled out this paper and I point down through the list. I said, "I meet these minimum requirements for the exam." Just about that time, a flight surgeon -- he was a Major, this guy was a captain. A major came back and he heard our argument.

"What's going on here?" Captain said, "We're not going to test this guy. We're not going to waste our time. He's too little." Major said, "Send him in." So I went in. I passed the test. I had 20/15 vision in both eyes. I mean -- and from a standpoint of being healthy, I was in superb shape. Didn't weigh very much, but I -- I had eaten six bananas and drank some water before I went in just to make the weight. But I came out of there 118 pounds and five-feet-four. And I got -- a couple of days later that I had passed the test and so on, and to "report to the old post office building on December 8 at eight o'clock in the morning. We will swear you in to the Air Corp." Ballard got the same notice.

He and I got on the bus Sunday morning, December 7th, around nine o'clock. We drove down to the -- the bus took us down to Pittsburgh. We got out, went to the William Penn Hotel. We got there about two o'clock in the afternoon. We walked into the room, put our duffel bags down, turned the radio on and at that moment, they were announcing Pearl Harbor.

That's where I was when they announced Pearl Harbor. At eight o'clock in the morning the next day, December 8th, 1941, I was sworn in to the U.S. Air Corp. And at noontime -- they gave us a big speech about what to expect and so on, and where we were going. And in the meantime, lunch hour came. We went across the street to a diner. And in that diner, there were stools around the -- where they served you. Ballard and I were sitting on our stools and having lunch when Franklin Roosevelt declared war on Japan. So to answer your question, that's where I was. Took a long time to get here, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's great. What were the reactions of the diners listening to the speech?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: In those days, everybody seemed to know it was coming, but they were devastated they had the gall to attack us. What in the world are those Japanese doing? There are two Japanese guys up in Washington saying, oh, we're going to make peace and so on, and in the meantime, they're attacking Hawaii. And we -- well, people were madder than a hornet and couldn't hardly stand it.

So anyhow, I went back to work because we didn't have to report immediately. And then we reported. And to tell you the truth -- this is a terrible thing to say, but Ballard and I left there and we went to Pittsburgh. At Pittsburgh, I was sent to Montgomery, Alabama. Ballard was sent out to, I think it was Kingston, California. Out in there, anyway. He and I both survived the war. He died on my birthday last year. I had never laid eyes on that guy since. We called each other on December 7th every year.

He went to work for Boeing when he came out, and stayed on the West Coast. And I never had an opportunity. Our paths never even got close. So I never saw him again. But he survived the war. He became a B-17 driver. He flew 28 missions out in England early in the war. He told me he splashed two of them in the drink coming back from -- he was flying B-17's, and he said he splashed two of them in the channel on the way back. But this guy, they all survived. And he went to work for Boeing. Became a civilian. Worked for Boeing and a couple of airplane supply places out there in the West Coast. And he retired from that. But I never laid eyes on him again. And that is a sad story on my part. But we talked. We talked on the phone. And we had a lot of conversations, but we never saw each other. So that brings you up to where I took my flight training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Montgomery; right?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: I went to Montgomery and that was pre-flight there. It was Southeast Air Corps Training Command. And I went to Montgomery. We took pre-flight. We went to Decatur, Alabama for primary. We went from Decatur to Blyth, Arkansas for basic, and to Craig Field, Selma, Alabama for advanced. And I graduated, got my wings and became a second lieutenant officer in the ORC, Officers Reserve Corp of the Air Corp on January 14th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particularly interesting stories of anything that happened during your training?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: I probably had more cushions on my seat than anybody had. And my parachute probably weighed the most because I had drags and everything stuffed in it so it would fit. I was told one time by some of the guys, "Carll, if you ever had to jump out of that airplane, that parachute will go up before it will come down." The guy was the instructor. His name was C.F. Lush. There were about five of us that were under Lush, and one of the guy's names was Bud Callen.

He was from South Dakota. Bud -- I don't know how he passed the physical or anything because his coordination was off quite a bit. Anyhow, he was always having a scrap with Lush. Lush sat in the front seat and the trainer -- the trainee was sitting in the rear seat of that. Callen said, "I wanted to grab that crank and hit him over the head, 'cause," he said, "he calls me every name in the book." Well, I never had that. I had a lot of scolding from him, "You're ten feet off," or you're this or that. It was all part of the training. But then Basic Benjamin A. Click, Jr. was the instructor, and he was a hay seed from Tennessee.

And when he would tell us what we were going to do, he'd stand there, his head down and he was always chewing on a piece of grass. And he'd take his foot and drag it across and say, "Now, this is what we're going to do today. We're going to do this," and he would describe our flight and what we were going to do by making a design on the dirt on the street. He was quite a guy and a good pilot. Wonderful pilot. And he taught us well. So I got through basic.

We went to advanced. We flew BT-13's. Full T-Vibrators is what we called it. And then we went to Craig Field, Selma, Alabama. We flew advanced in a North American AT6. Pretty uneventful as far as I was concerned. We went through, we did all kinds of things with the airplane. Graduated in January of '43, in the class of '43A.

And then they transferred us from there to Sarasota, Florida to OTU. In those days, it was called OTU, which was operational training unit. And we took OTU in P-40's. My instructor, now there is a fellow that I still keep in contact with. He's four years older than I am. He lives in Florida. But his name is Chester L. Van Etton. And on his airplane when he was flying combat says "mayor of all California."

Anyhow, he was one -- he is one fantastic guy. Absolutely. He joined the RAF, not RCAF, RAF. And he was 16 years old and he flew in the Battle of Britain. And then when the United States entered the war, he transferred from the English RAF, into the U.S. Air Corp. He'd already flown in the Battle of Britain. And he was an instructor down at Sarasota and he was my instructor.

I'll tell you, that guy could teach you how to fly. We flew the tightest formation of anybody. I remember when he first took me up, he said, "We're going to fly close formation today." I thought I was in tight. Because I could handle an airplane by that time, and I thought I was in tight. I'd look up there to him and he'd say, "Bring it in. Bring it in." He wasn't satisfied until I had that wing right up against the star on the side of the airplane and my prop about that far behind the aileron. I mean ... so one time, I said, "How come we have to fly this close?"

He was smoothest. He was very smooth on the throttle. You could almost set your throttle and squeeze -- and tighten up the throttle because he'd fly that way all day long. And you could hang in there. I mean, you could hang in there tight. You weren't one of these throttle jockeys just laying that way and having to make your own adjustments, you know. Anyhow, he told me, he says, "I'll tell you, Carll, you better learn to fly this formation tight because there will be times in weather where the weather is so rotten that even if you're flying this tight, you'll won't even be able to see your number four airplane."

And he said, "My suggestion to you is if you -- if you ever have anybody to look after, teach them how to fly this, this tight." So I took his word for it. Anyhow, got through that OTU, and we finished that up in March, early March. And we were sent to Miami -- actually, in Boca Raton, in preparation to go overseas. And if you have time, this is another fantastic story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I've got lots of time.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: We were billeted at the Battle Creek Hotel at Boca Raton, Florida, and two of us lined up to go overseas. And part of our group was from Luke Field, Arizona. And, of course, others were Craig Field. About half-and-half. And we were billeted there just waiting on airplanes to take us. We finally got boarded, we were going to ship out. In the Battle Creek Hotel, the big lobby down in the front of it was where they asked us to put our gear. And our gear consists of a big B-4 bag with our clothes; parachute bag, which was about two and a half feet long and probably 14 inches on a side, square, 15. It carried a parachute and your heavy, high-altitude flying jacket and your goggles and all the equipment to fly an airplane was in that parachute bag.

Then we had a little bag of security, musette bag, carried a musette bag. And that was our gear. Well, in those days, you had to be very careful about weight on these airplanes, commercial airlines. I think Pan Am was supplying the C-54's. In those days, it was a DC-4, and they had arranged it for a long-range.

Anyhow, on this particular day, we were going to ship out at nine o'clock in the evening. On this particular day at four o'clock, they said, "We will pick you up in front of the hotel, take you down and weigh you guys with everything you're going to carry." So in my case, it was my musette bag and me. I was going to ship all the rest of it, because I had my shaving stuff and change of underwear and that sort of thing in that musette bag. Anyhow, this we did.

We went down and we had -- we were down there probably an hour. Came back. Maybe we got back about 5:00, 5:30. When we came back, I went over to where I had my gear stashed. It was kind of in the outside of the pile and my parachute bag was open. About -- the zipper was open about a foot or 15 inches, something like that. I was puzzled for a little bit, but then I just zipped it back up and didn't think anymore about it. We were all then to go to mess. Mess was at six o'clock. So we all go to mess.

While we were going to mess, the crew was coming in, picking up our bags and going down and loading the airplanes so we would have an eight o'clock take-off. The problem -- up to that time, there were no problems, but shortly after six -- and I was sitting way in the back of the room with the other guys and the room was full, there was a Major came in and over the PA system, he said, "Is there a Lieutenant Carll in this room?" So I stood up, I said, "Yes." I was immediately grabbed by two big M.P.'s about six feet tall, taken out of that lunch hall and taken down the hall and put in a room. And what had happened was -- make a long story short.

What had happened was when they were loading the airplane, the sergeant picked up my parachute bag. And when he picked it up on the straps and was pushing it into the shelf on this C-54, the end of it was hot. So he took it to the door, threw it out on the ground and it burst into flames. And it was my bag. What had happened was, it turned out -- the Battle Creek Hotel in Boca Raton, Florida was completely infested with German spies that had been dumped off along the shore by a German submarine and gone in and they had infiltrated Miami Airport and all along the coast there.

And three weeks before our airplane left, another C-54 left with 32 guys on it and never was heard from. We didn't know this until after, but -- I didn't take off with those guys at eight o'clock. I was interrogated by the FBI, the OSS. By midnight that night, there were two generals of the Air Force down in Washington, D.C. and they really grilled me through the mill and so on. It turns out while I was there, the FBI even went back to my home and searched and asked neighbors and so on what kind of a guy I was and all that. But they left. And it could have been disastrous because in a C-54 -- DC-4 in those days -- it was not a long-range aircraft when they built it for commercial use. It was going to be used just in the United States. But to make it a long-range transport, they put behind the bulkhead -- here is the pilots' compartment. Behind the bulkhead, they put two horizontal tanks that contained a hundred octane gasoline, long-range tanks. And they were stacked on top of each other. But from the bulkhead to the end of the first tank, there were shelves and that's where part of the gear was. Then there was a second bulkhead -- and this was kind of a middle compartment in that. There was a second bulkhead and at the other end of this gas tank, there were shelves built. And so this was where the gear was stored and you could put all of the 32 guys' gear in those shelves in there. But it was right in there next to those hundred octane gas tanks. And my bag would have been within one foot of that, because as they were coming down, that's where my bag would have been. So the good Lord was looking after us. Anyhow --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So had they put something, lit something on fire? What happened?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: No. It turns out, after the investigation, they had like a sheet of phosphorescent paper, like eight-and-a-half by 11 or something, and all they had to do was open up a bag and slip it down inbetween, and that was designed to catch on fire in eight hours. It turned out that this had caught on fire in much less than eight hours. So are you ready for another side on this?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: There's a lot of detail, but it is an interesting story. On the day before -- the day before that we were going to ship out, they told us to go to the Quartermaster and collect our money. So a good friend of mine, George Bludnik, we'd been through flight school together, we were to go down to Quartermaster and pick up our pay. It was $80. We came back and Bludnik said to me, he said, "Carll, how much money did you get?" I said, "I got the same amount you got. I got 80 bucks."

He said, "How about loaning me the 80 bucks?" Because he said, "They're going to give us freedom to go into town tonight," and he said, "I think I'd like to go into town," but he said, "I'll need some money." He was a gambler and everything else. I said, "Well, George, I'll tell you what. 80 bucks, that's all I have, but I'll loan you 75."

So I got five bucks. So this occurred the night before. With all this excitement and so on, I never thought about that money. But I had five dollars in my pocket. Well, those guys left. And I'm here with five dollars and I'm under house arrest. And while I'm under house arrest, the government pays everything. They feed you. They pay your hotel bill. All of this. So this interrogation went on for about five days. Finally, they said, "Carll, you're completely exonerated from any of this stuff. Go ahead and" -- but they'd confiscated all my gear. I didn't have a damn thing. Nothing. Not even my musette bag. They confiscated all of that for testing.

And they picked the wrong guy, whoever put that paper in there, because I didn't smoke, I didn't drink, I didn't have any of those problems. So my bags were completely cleared of anything burnable, except a can of Kiwi shoe polish. That was the only thing that burned. Anyhow, he said, "You're free to go. Go over and report to the base commander. Go to Quartermaster and get re-supplied with your gear," and so on. When I left Miami, the base commander said, "I want you to meet sergeant" so-and-so. "He's carrying very secret papers to be delivered. He's going to take them over to Cairo. But what I want you to do is to be responsible for this sergeant and carry these papers, these documents." And he gave me a brown envelope with them all in there. On the outside was "secret," which was top classified information, in red.

"I want you to deliver this to the base commander at Natel, Brazil, the sergeant and the documents." So the sergeant sat right beside me on this flight. I always wondered, never knew, always wondered if he was an FBI guy or somebody that was looking after -- who was looking after whom or was -- you know. Anyhow, we got down to Natel. And I went in. I took the sergeant and went in. I should tell you that I put these papers inside my shirt and I never took them out until I got into the base commander's office down in Natel.

And I went in there and saluted the guy behind the desk and told him I was carrying some information that I need to pass on to him. And I pulled this out of my shirt, handed it to him. And I said, "And sergeant" so-and-so. I had his name, I don't remember what it was. I said, "I'm supposed to turn these over to you. They're under your jurisdiction now." And I stood there at attention. And he said -- I never moved, he said, At ease." He says, "You're excused." I said, "Sir, if you don't mind, I'd like to have a receipt for this." He gave me a receipt. So I excused myself and left.

Well, a few days later, we left and we were flying this southern Pan Am route. We left in a DC-3. And we got airborne and I was sitting up. The DC-3 had these seats up along the side and on the back end. There weren't that many of us in the airplane, maybe ten guys or so, but it was full of other gear and stuff, piles of cargo. Anyhow, I'm sitting up on this bench and I had a paperback book, I guess, I was reading. Next thing I know, here come a Major. He come up through there. We had been up over the water maybe an hour, hour and a half, something like that.

He said, "Lieutenant, we need another guy in the back. They've got a big poker game going on," and he said, "we need another guy." I said, "Major, I don't play cards. In the first place, I don't even know how to play Poker. I don't even know any of these cards. He said, "We need another guy." And he's a major, you know. I'm just a second "Louie," which had been battered for a couple of weeks in very strange circumstances. I just wanted to be left alone. But, anyhow, he wouldn't leave me alone. So I went back. And here, here is this full-bird Colonel. I mean, this poker game had all these guys. And there's a blanket on the floor, they're playing cards and everybody's -- and they invited me in, treated me like a king. I mean really. And everybody out-ranked me by a couple of grades anyway. And I sat right beside this Colonel, this full Colonel.

We played cards until we got to Ascension Island. And by the time we got to Ascension Island, I had won 39 dollars. I didn't know anything. I'm sure these guys, these old-timers kept feeding me, letting me win. So we got to Ascension Island and I couldn't believe it that I was this wealthy. We go up to Acraw on the Gold Coast, and then we went to Legos, Nigeria. And this is where those guys -- most of those guys were going. Well, in Legos, they had a P-40 shop where they re-assembled P-40's that were shipped in, in crates. And then guys were supposed to fly them up across. Well, I reported in there because they said they needed pilots to fly them up across Africa to Cairo. It turned out the way they did that -- nobody had the navigational equipment in those days. So if there was a B-20 or B-25 going to Russia, why they would do the navigating and you would just fly the P-40, fly their wing and so on. Well, it turned out they didn't have anybody there to -- at that time. So they said -- he says, "You're going to have to find your way to Cairo any way you can." So I tacked on to a DC-3. And we went from -- I was just -- I was alone and I was kind of a bum, you know, but I got this ride on this DC-3. It was a mail plane.
(END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE)

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: We left Legos and we flew to Cano, Nigeria. And then from Cano, we went to Meduri. Somewhere along in there, it was hotter than Hades. DC-3 flew about 9-, 10,000 feet, rougher than a cobb. I mean, it was really up and down and all -- it was a rough trip. And I'm on the back end of this thing and over the PA system, the pilot comes on, and he said -- and everybody around me was sick. I wasn't sick, but everybody around. This guy come over the PA system, "Is there anybody in the back end there that's not sick?" He said, "If there is, come on up here." Well, it was a pilot. His copilot was sick as a dog and was of no use to him.

And he had thrown up all over the inside of that thing. Finally, he was, you know, awake enough to get the heck out of there, but he didn't clean up his mess. So the pilot said to me, he said, "Well, why don't you try and clean this up a little bit." And we opened up the windows to try to get the odor out, you know. So anyhow, I wound up being the copilot on that DC-3 and we flew it all the way up to Cairo, this guy and I.

And we stopped at El Fassur and Khartoum and Luxor and Cairo. And we got into Cairo at the Heady Office Airport, and that was as far as he was going. So I had to go over to El Cabrit. That's where my orders were cut for, and that was over on the Suez Canal. So I bummed a ride over there. I went over there on a GI truck. Finally got to where I was supposed to go. They had a training unit. 57th Fighter Group had a training unit there. Dave Hartman and Charlie Feroham were running it. And I reported in. And that's where I caught up with all the rest of my guys and Bludnik finally paid me my 75 bucks. But, anyhow, we were there for about a week or so. And then they -- and then we went up to the front lines. So that's how I got into combat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go to front lines? Approximately, when would that be?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: I got in the front lines in April.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: April of '44?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Of '43. April of '43. Now, the 57th Fighter Group was the very first American group into the desert theater over there. In February of 1942, Winston Churchill came over here and got ahold of Roosevelt and begged him for help, absolutely begged him for help. Well, Curtiss Wright had an order from Britain for 100 P-40 airplanes, the F model.

The reason for the F model was, it was powered by the Rolls Royce Merlin engine built by Rolls Royce. And these 100 aircraft were supposed to go to the China-Burma theater, over into Burma. Churchill was successful in talking Roosevelt to give help. The 57th Fighter Group had not been informed. They cobbled together the 57th Fighter Group up in Windsor Lock, Connecticut, out of the old Eighth Pursuit Group, a couple of 33rd. I was with Phil Cochran, Johnny Allison, Buck Doolby, Barnum, Frank, those guys.

And what they did was, instead of sending those hundred P-40F to England -- or to Burma, they diverted them to New York. They painted them desert pink and took those pink P-40's, threw them down to Long Island, loaded them onto the USS Ranger. And in July of 1942, the USS Ranger with 72 P-40F's and our 57th Fighter Group on board, the pilots, they went down and about a hundred miles off of the Gold Coast, they flew off that carrier, USS Ranger, and went up to Acraw on the Gold Coast and then across Africa. And they wound up to -- wound up in Palestine. They got up to Palestine, August, September of 1942.

U.S. did not have an Air Force or an Air Corp unit over there. We were assigned to the RAF. We were kind of -- we were kind of a bastard outfit, if you will. Excuse the language, but that's what it was. Anyhow, we were attached to the RAF. And the English designation was Desert Air Force. So the 57th Fighter Group flew along with 239 Wing of the RAF and we were in the Desert Air Force. And it wasn't until March of 1943 that the Ninth Air Force set up headquarters in Cairo.

And at that time, administratively, we were under the Ninth Air Force, U.S. but we took our operational -- all of our intelligence and everything was British, and we flew behind the British Eighth Army going up across Africa and so on. I got there in April, up at the front lines. Carwun, Elgin or Carwun, I'm not ... I think it was Carwun, Indonesia. On April 18th, 1943 was the Palm Sunday Massacre. The Palm Sunday Massacre was the 57th Fighter Group intercepted a huge German convoy of aircraft coming in to supply the Germans. JU-52's were the cargo planes. They were escorted by ME-109's. Our group shot down 76 airplanes in ten minutes. We devastated the German -- that whole thing. You could see aircraft hulls burning three or four days later that had made sure and so on.

Anyhow, later on in the war, they shot down 90 Japanese airplanes in one day, but the Marines, Navy, the Air Force and everybody was involved in it, and they said that's the greatest. In ten minutes, our guys shot down 76 German airplanes. This was April 18th.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was this your first combat mission then?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: No, I wasn't on that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you weren't on that mission.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: I was in the outfit, but I wasn't on the mission.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Those old hands were on it. And on May 5th, 1943, just a couple of weeks after that, the Germans evacuated North Africa. We think that was the deciding blow, and we made it. If you read history of Montgomery's march up through there, we are never mentioned. We are never, ever mentioned. We flew behind the British Eighth Army all the way through Sicily, Italy. And we were still behind the British Eighth Army in December of '43. We had -- we were interdicting German supply routes across the Adriatic Sea into Yugoslavia. We had a lot of missions going into Yugoslavia to keep that supply route of German -- have it -- we shut it down, actually.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first combat mission? Do you have specific memories of that?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Yeah, I do. It was -- it was a target of opportunity. The Germans were still on -- in Tunisia, but they were pretty well whipped. It was a strafing mission up in Tunisia there. Kind of uneventful.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not a lot of opposition from the air?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: No, we didn't have -- not at that point. And -- they were getting ready to leave. I mean, it was just ... they didn't want anymore of us guys. Anyhow, we had -- we then, from those bases, we started and flew over Panaleria. That's an island in between Sicily and Africa. And I flew missions over that, dive-bomb missions and so forth. And the island, they surrendered. The Germans surrendered. It's the only time, the first time that the Air Force was surrendered to and there were no infantry or anybody involved on land.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Which island was this again?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Panaleria.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Panaleria. And the Germans had hangars built on the side of the hills there and we weren't the only ones dive bombing, P-38's. P-38 guys came and they threw bombs in the hangar doors. We actually almost blew the place down, you know. But they surrendered in a few days. Well, they pulled us back to Kosway in Libya, near Tripoli. And we were there just kind of waiting for the invasion of Sicily. And then we waited there for a while. It was kind of a staging area, I guess. And then they moved us to Malta. And we flew a few missions from Malta to soften up the southern coast of Sicily.

Then on D plus 4, they moved us into Pashino, Sicily, right on the tip, right down on the tip. The Germans were seven miles up the road. At night-time you could hear all of the war going on and so forth. I mean -- but I'll tell you what Tom, even down in Africa, we'd move up -- we were moving real fast. We'd move up and many times we'd be maybe two or three miles behind the lines. And then the Germans would move on. So it was a chase, really.

The invasion of Sicily was a disaster. Nervous guys shot down 23 DC-3's that were going in there with parachute -- paratroopers in it. Those poor paratroopers were scattered all over the southern end of Sicily. We had them coming into our camp just trying to get up to their outfits, you know. So we flew missions, chasing -- the British Eighth Army went up the east side of Sicily and the landings were Patton's outfit and they went up through ... oh, around on the west side of the islands, you know.

Palermo. They went up through Palermo Road. We went up through Katania, Augusta, Syracuse, that way, toward Messina. And the next place we stopped was Escordia, Sicily. Jerry Brandon and I, we were the very first two guys to land on Escordia strip. But we came into, he said -- I want you -- he said, to Jerry, he said, "Brandon," he said, "I want you and Carll to go out and check out that field before the rest of us come on up." So he and I were the very first two guys on Escordia landing ground. And we flew in there and we reported back to them. It looked like it was okay. And they moved on up. The Eighth party came and so forth. But we stayed in Escordia for quite a while.

Finally, we drove the Germans out across the Messina straits and we were still in Escordia. And then the Salerno landings. Now, if you take a look at the map from Sicily to Naples, that is across an awful lot of water, and we supported those landings from Escordia. We had to load up with bombs and everything and go to the northern edge of Sicily land at an air base, top off our fuel tanks and fly up to Salerno dive bombing and strafing. That's what we did. And Stromboli, that island that's erupting over there even today, was landmarked. You could see it for miles. And if you went right across Stromboli, you could hit right down to Escordia. So we did that. Then we drove the Germans out of Sicily completely. We were still with the British Eighth Army and we went over to Rocko Bernardo which is on the instep of the boot. Very quickly, very quickly, the bomb line became out of range for us. So we had to move on up. We went up to Joya, which is northwest of Berry. And we flew a few missions from there. And then we moved us right into Foggia, because the British Eighth Army was really chasing the Germans out of that whole thing and they didn't have a whole lot of support.

Most of the Germans were over on against Mark Clark. Do you know where the Wall Tower River was the bomb line for them, and they couldn't shake that. Well, we didn't -- we were interdicting supply lines in Yugoslavia and flying over there and on up north on the east side. December ... December about the third week in December, we got P-47's. We'd been flying P-40's. And they were brand-new P-47's came in there. And then for about two weeks, three weeks, we didn't know what we were going to fly, whether it was a P-40 or P-47 in the transition.
But we were flying over to -- have a break-through in the Voltaro River and then the Anzio Beachhead, which was a deadly place. We lost a lot of pilots in that deal. Then --

I should tell you another story. In September, it was the third week in September or so, we were in Anandola, which was southeast of Foggia near Macedonia. We had a mission. It was a mission of opportunity, target of opportunity. I was -- at the briefing, Art Exxon, he was going to be the lead guy and I was leading Yellow Section, which is the mid section. And I think Lou Mastry was leading the top section, Red Section. Anyhow, as we were flying north -- this was like 5:30 in the morning. As we were flying north, we spotted a live train going north, just south of Ancona. And Art Exxon was our call -- our call was Hitchhike. He was Hitchhike Leader and I was Yellow Section. At the briefing, he said that when we had a target of opportunity, he would call the sections he wanted to go down on it. Well, we were going along there. We were flying north. So at three o'clock was where the target of opportunity was. And it was this train going. So he called Yellow Section. He said, "We'll cover. You go down and take -- that's the target." So when you -- any time you're attacking a railroad train, a train that's on a railroad, you go across it 90 degrees to how it's traveling so that you're over the cars the least amount of time. Anyhow, we went down and the train was just pulling into the Anacona station. And as we went over it, the boxcars were empty. They had doors open and you could see right through it. But anyhow, we were lined up to work on the live trains. We shot up the back-end cars. We went over the train, and I called Art, I said, "Hitchhike Leader," I said, "the northbound train is empty, but the train on the siding, there are trucks and that train along siding is full. So we'll do a 180, come back and get the engine, and then I'll cover -- we'll cover you guys."

So we did 180, we came back. I can truthfully say that I got that engine. I blew the engine up. And I can say that because I was the first one over. Every other time that we ever hit anything like that, I was way down the line, but I blew that one up. One of the guys, you know, "Good show." There was a lot of ... we pulled off of that flight, and Art had -- Abercrombie was flying his wing. Moe Raskin was leading the element. And his was the only airplane that had a camera in it that day. First day, we ever had cameras in the P-40's. And Jimmy Moore was flying Moe's wing. Well, we pulled off the target. Made a wide sweeping left turn. And I was about 3,000 feet, I think, when this tremendous explosion took place. The mushroom cloud, that was the biggest thing I had ever seen. And I believe it was the biggest thing until the atomic bomb went off in Japan that ever went. The cloud was -- went up over 12,000 feet. It was huge. And I only saw three airplanes coming out of the other side.

I called Art, and I said, "You've lost your No. 4 man." You know, "Hitchhike Leader, you've lost your No. 4 man." And it was Jimmy Moore. Jimmy Moore said, "I'm still here. I'm here," he says. He told me later that this thing blew up right in front of him and he pulled back on the stick and he said he was going almost straight up. And there were trucks, boxcar trucks and sides of boxcars going up with him in this explosion. It was huge. And the thing got Raskin. He was right over it when it blew. But the other two guys went through. So Art said, "Well, I'll check." So he did a 180 and he came by. And just about the time he hit there again, there was another humungous explosion, and it missed him. But he went back, but he couldn't find any airplane that was down. But anyhow, Moe bought the farm that day.

There were two Spitfires about 50 to 100 miles north of there that they were on a wrecking mission. And this was such a huge explosion that they flew down and they took some photographs. We blew up 23 boxcars of cordite. 52 trucks that were in there were obliterated. About three-quarters of a mile of track was blown up and the entire station was demolished. That whole thing blew up.

Within a very short time after that, they moved us over to Sercola at the foot of Mt. Vesuvius to support the Fifth Army and the Americans, because that seemed to be the death knell of the Germans on that side. But the truth of the matter is, we dealt them a very devastating blow that morning. Never written up anyplace. Nothing was ... you know, some of the things we did have never been told. I don't know, I've told this story a couple of times, maybe half a dozen times to other people, but to tell it to you, I'm sure that that story hasn't been told. But it was a devastating blow to the Germans on the east side of Italy.

And shortly thereafter, they moved us over to the west side of Italy and we started supporting Mark Clark and the Fifth Army. We were there for about, I don't know, maybe a week or two. Mt. Vesuvius erupted while we were there. And the 324th Bomb Group -- the 324th Bomb Group, they are on the east side of Vesuvius. And the wind was blowing such and the hot ashes came down and wiped out the whole entire airplane deal there. Of course, the commander got fired and so on, but it did it. It dealt a devastating blow to our medium bomb group in that area there.

Anyhow, very shortly after that, we got orders to move from Naples or Sercola there, to Corsica. And our job was Operation Strangle. Operation Strangle was to keep the rail lines cut traveling south so that the Germans couldn't supply. And when you look at a map, we were up near Bashu, about 15 miles south of Bashu to an air base we called Alto. A-l-t-o. We started flying on this project and we successfully cut the rail lines across Italy, all the way across Italy.

Now, later on some medium bomb groups and some -- but we were the first group to get up there on that job. And we had an interesting case. We'd come back with our reconnaissance and tell them -- tell the intelligence people they're cut, all the bridges. We'd knocked all the bridges out and so on. Answer came back, says, "You guys are nuts. You haven't cut them all. They're getting lined." They told us what line was open and it was going down south and so forth. And that they were still getting deliveries over that line. We said we couldn't believe it because it was a huge bridge out that we'd knocked, you know. So anyhow, we flew over there one morning about early in the morning. It was still dusk. It hadn't -- dawn hadn't even shown up yet. And what we spotted was these blooming Germans had a section of rail on trucks. And they pulled that thing into a tunnel that was about a mile away from that thing, and they hid it in a tunnel during the daytime. At night-time, they ran that section out, bridged that with a section of rail and all night long, they ran trains back and forth across it.

And then -- well, when we discovered that, we weren't the only ones. They brought in the P-38's too. But what we did was we skip-bombed thousand pounders into the mouth of that tunnel. And I don't know how much damage we did, but we finally did knock that line out. But the Germans were very ingenious.

We had another case where they -- it was across the river. All the bridges were out. And you fly over that thing and you couldn't see how in the world they were delivering anything. But they claim, oh, the trucks are getting through. Trucks are getting through. It turns out that what those Germans had done was they paved a road that was about two feet underneath the surface of the river. And they drove across that road and you fly over it. The river was still running. There's no bridge there, but it was underneath the surface of the water and those rascals -- well, you know, every time we found something like that, well, we tried to make sure it didn't work. But that's what we are up against. The Germans were very ingenious. And we have to give them credit, they knew what the heck they were doing.

Anyhow, Tom, we flew off of Alto there. And that was our job. I think Operation Strangle was pretty effective. I think we were pretty effective in it. And by that -- I'd been a flight leader for quite a while, but I drew the short straw to fly the very first mission into southern France to start to soften up the landing area in southern France. Another side story on that thing. If you notice how Corsica is shaped, there's a finger that sticks up like this, you know, and we were based over here on this side. Well, the briefing was to fly up here, then take a heading north of this point and land over toward Nice. Fly that heading and then return the same. Well, this was kind of late in the afternoon and none of us knew. We had a rough estimation of what the flight time would be but -- and we were flying Thunderbolts. So we flew the route over there and we went over and we bombed some shipping that was in a cove near Nice and strafed a couple of things down along the thing and we turned around and come back. But by this time, it's getting late in the evening. So I'm in charge of the thing. So I called the guys, and I said, "We're flying to -- we'll climb to 14-5 and we'll go directly over the mountains and let down on the other side and come in. Mountains are 14,000 feet high over there. So that was the quickest way back, so that's what we did.

We flew over the mountains and spiraled down and landed in Alto. That night, the Germans, they had a station over on the island of Alba and there are much U-boats over there. And these U-boats, actually, they came over. And, you know, they floated or powered, whatever they did, up along the east coast of Corsica and shelled our air bases. They had 88's mounted on these things and they were shelling these air bases. Well, our flight was the last flight in that night and our route was supposed to be down, you know, same way we went out, which I didn't come back that way. So next morning, I get called in on the carpet.

The old man says, "Why didn't you see those U-boats?" He says, "They caused a lot of trouble here." Started giving me the what for. And I said to him, I said, "Colonel, I didn't come back that route. I said, "It was getting dark and we flew a direct line to our air base over the mountains and spiraled down and I brought them in." I said, "All 12 of us got back okay," and so on. "We never were out over the water at all and we did not see them." He said, "That's fine." That was all I ever heard of it.

But you see, the guy in charge of the flight, it was up to him to decide what he wanted to do, you know. I had the final say and that's respected, in the Air Force respected. Well, I had the final say. I explained to him that I came back over the mountains because it was the quickest way home and I was wanting to get home before dark. That was the answer to it. But that was -- see how things happen that are a little unusual, you know. Well, then, you know, I wound up my tour and I got home on June 2nd of 1944, I came home. I could tell you this, while our outfit was up there on Alto Air Base on Corsica, movie director, William Wyler, came over and he wanted to photograph a mission and that sort of thing. Abercrombie, who was my tent mate, he flew our B-25's that kept William Wyler's photography crew and so on. And they photographed like Squadron going out on a mission and so on. And it is in "Thunderbolt," that the -- if you have "Thunderbolt" --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: That was made by William Wyler. And my guys -- the 64 Squadron isn't shown too much in there. We were the Black Scorpions. But 66 and 65 are shown, the Fighting Cocks, Phil Cochran's outfit. And Abercrombie, who lives today in Minneapolis, he and I were tent mates all through the war, he flew the B-25's that took those.

While he was there, William Wyler interviewed our guys in all of our squadrons. Our squadron 64, 65, 66. And they took copious notes. And when he came back, the movie, "The Best Years of Our Lives," it's based on that, on those interviews. And that's where that came from. So, while we never got much recognition, we were, in my view, and not because I belonged to the outfit, but in my view, we did our job and we did a great job. And that's pretty much the story of the 57th Fighter Group. Now, is there anything else?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you married at the time when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: No, I wasn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a girl back home or anything?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting mail, mail call, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Paul L. Carll
sp.p: Always. She was great, my wife upstairs. I came home on June 2nd and I had flown well over a hundred missions, which was quite a lot of missions for those days. Anyhow, I got home. I was on a 21-day pass. I got home on the 2nd. We had figured we were going to get married. I had to go to the county courthouse and Judge McCracken was the county judge. I went in there to get a marriage license. And he looked at me, and he said, "I don't think you want to do this." And I had a couple of those ribbons, you know, and so on. I was in uniform. And he said, "I don't think you want to do this." And I said, "Why?" He said, "You know, son, you're in an awful dangerous business." I said, "We waited long enough. We're going to get married."

This is another thing you will not believe. We were married on D-Day, June 6th, 1944. I'd been over there and back and so on. My brother had saved some gas stamps, so I borrowed his car and our honeymoon was Niagara Falls. And we drove from Wall City, Pennsylvania, to Niagara Falls. We are up there a couple of days. Came back home and there was a telegram waiting for me to report immediately to Atlantic City. So I didn't even have my 21 days. So I took Marian with me.

We went over to Atlantic City, and I had to send her home because I was in secret orders to go to Eglin Field, Florida. The project was a special project. There were nine of us and we were on ultra-secret orders. And the project was to select the armament and work out the flight path that would knock out the V-1 launchers from Belgium that were dropping on London.
(END OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE)
